author: nathan-hewitt
description: Between 1845 and 1852, a million Irish people starved to death while ships loaded with grain and livestock left their ports. Two historians clash over what that paradox means.

hero.hook: A million dead, and ships loaded with grain and cattle still sailing out of Irish ports.

blocks.text: Between **1845** and **1852**, the [[Great Famine]] killed about **a million** people in Ireland. The trigger was [[potato blight]], a fungus-like mold that destroyed the crops and robbed the country of its most important food. Yet while Irish people starved, grain, livestock and butter kept leaving Irish ports on British ships, bound for British tables.

How could a country export food while it was starving? The question has haunted historians and Irish people ever since. Two readings stand opposed. The first sees these exports as a symbol of British exploitation. The second sees them as only one piece of a far more complicated picture, made of exports but also of imports.

In the 19th century, the potato was the staple of the Irish diet. It provided cheap calories and needed little land. Poor farmers could therefore use the rest of their plot for other crops or livestock, sold for cash to pay the rent, mostly to English landlords. Much of that surplus already ended up in Britain: Ireland was then governed from London, as part of the United Kingdom.

When the blight struck in **1845**, it destroyed up to **50%** of the national potato crop. Ireland slid into catastrophe. Yet the exports went on. They were organized by British and Irish merchants, not by the government in London. But the government refused to stop them: in the name of the [[free market]], it judged that any interference would only make things worse.

The blight did not hit Ireland alone: it ravaged potato fields across Europe and North America. Ireland was by far the worst affected, but Belgium, Germany and Scotland also counted tens of thousands of deaths.

For historians such as [[Christine Kinealy]], these exports made the famine worse. She calculated that **430,000 tons** of grain left Ireland between 1846 and 1847, along with almost **half a million pigs** and a quarter of a million sheep. Shipments of butter and eggs never stopped during the famine years.

blocks.caption: A funeral at Skibbereen, County Cork: engraving after H. Smith for the Illustrated London News, January 1847.

blocks.text: That food could have fed up to **2 million** people for **16 months**, enough to blunt the famine's worst effects. But the merchants chose profit over human life: instead of sending these goods to those who needed them, they sold them to those who could pay the most. By letting the exports continue, Kinealy concludes, Britain indirectly caused the famine.

Other historians, such as [[James Donnelly]], challenge this reading. During the famine years, he points out, Ireland imported more food from Britain than it exported. In **1847** and **1848**, more than **1.3 million tons** of grain came into the country, over three times what went out. And even if every ton of exported grain had stayed in Ireland, it would have filled only part of the gap.

Blocking exports would not have guaranteed that food reached the starving either. The regions that exported were generally not the ones hit hardest. Grain held back in County Tyrone, in the north of the island, would not necessarily have ended up on the tables of the dying in County Mayo, on the west coast.

The famine was a turning point for the Irish people. **A million** dead, and as many as **2 million** emigrants, most of them bound for the United States or Britain. The ordeal bound the survivors together. Unity in suffering, and anger at the British response, paved the way toward independence.

blocks.caption: The replica of the Jeanie Johnston, a three-masted ship that carried emigrants during the Great Famine, moored on the Liffey in Dublin.

blocks.text: The Irish nationalist [[John Mitchel]] summed up that anger in a famous line: "The Almighty sent the potato blight, but the English created the famine." Few historians today believe that Britain wanted the famine. But what it did, and what it failed to do, remains controversial. The Great Famine still weighs on relations between London and Dublin.
